trial_name: CATIS — Immediate Blood Pressure Reduction in Acute Ischemic Stroke (2014)
subtopic: Blood Pressure Management in Acute Ischemic Stroke
citation: He J, Zhang Y, Xu T, et al; CATIS Investigators. Effects of Immediate Blood Pressure Reduction on Death and Major Disability in Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: The CATIS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2014;311(5):479-489.
one_liner: In non-thrombolysed acute ischaemic stroke with SBP 140–<220 mm Hg, immediate BP reduction did not improve death or major disability at 14 days or 3 months.

pico.population: Adults ≥22 years with acute ischaemic stroke confirmed by CT/MRI, randomisation within 48 hours, systolic BP 140 to <220 mm Hg
pico.intervention: Immediate discontinuation of pre-stroke antihypertensives, then protocolised antihypertensive treatment targeting SBP reduction 10%–25% in first 24 hours, then <140/<90 mm Hg within 7 days and maintained
pico.comparison: Temporary discontinuation of all pre-stroke antihypertensives during hospitalisation, with no antihypertensive treatment unless clinically required outside trial
pico.outcome: Death or major disability (modified Rankin Scale 3–6) at 14 days or hospital discharge, whichever came first; also at 3 months

background.existing_knowledge: Elevated BP is common in the first hours–days after acute ischaemic stroke and is observationally associated with both favourable and unfavourable outcomes depending on timing, stroke subtype, and reperfusion status. Prior small trials of early BP modulation were inconclusive.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether early BP reduction improves outcomes compared with temporarily withholding antihypertensives in acute ischaemic stroke.
background.hypothesis: Immediate protocolised antihypertensive treatment would reduce death or major disability compared with temporary discontinuation.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, single-blind, blinded end-point trial

inclusion: Acute ischaemic stroke confirmed by CT/MRI
Randomisation within 48 hours of symptom onset
exclusion: Systolic BP ≥220 mm Hg or diastolic BP ≥120 mm Hg
Major comorbid cardiovascular instability (e.g., acute myocardial infarction/unstable angina, heart failure)
Other conditions judged to mandate urgent BP treatment

methods.intervention: Discontinuation of pre-stroke antihypertensives then immediate protocolised antihypertensive treatment. Targets: reduce SBP by 10%–25% within first 24 hours; achieve SBP/DBP <140/<90 mm Hg within 7 days and maintain during hospitalisation. Stepwise, centre-protocol using commonly available agents.
methods.comparison: Temporary discontinuation of all pre-stroke antihypertensives during hospitalisation, with no antihypertensive treatment unless clinically required outside trial framework.
methods.blinding: Treating clinicians unblinded; patients and outcome assessors blinded; outcomes adjudicated by blinded end-point committee.
methods.sample_size_power: 4000 planned to detect 5% absolute reduction (from 35% to 30%) with 90% power at 5% two-sided significance, allowing ~8% non-adherence/loss.
methods.primary_outcome: Death or major disability (mRS 3–6) at 14 days or hospital discharge, whichever came first.
secondary_outcomes: Death or major disability at 3 months
Systolic blood pressure at various time points
methods.follow_up: 14 days or hospital discharge (whichever came first) and 3 months post-randomisation.

headline_bullets: Protocolised BP reduction achieved sustained SBP separation of ~8–9 mm Hg in-hospital.
No difference in primary outcome: 33.6% vs 33.6% (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.88–1.14, P=.98).
Subgroup by time to randomisation suggested possible benefit when treatment started ≥24 h after onset (OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.55–0.97, P=.03).

outcomes_table.outcome: Systolic BP at 24 h, mean (SD), mm Hg
Systolic BP at day 7, mean (SD), mm Hg
Systolic BP at day 14, mean (SD), mm Hg
Primary: death or major disability (mRS 3–6) at 14 days/discharge
mRS shift (odds of 1-unit higher mRS) at 14 days/discharge
Systolic BP reduction from baseline at 24h, mean (SD), mm Hg
Systolic BP at 3 months, mean (SD), mm Hg

outcomes_table.note: More patients on BP therapy at follow-up in intervention arm

outcomes_table.outcome: Death or major disability (mRS 3–6) at 3 months

subgroup_table.subgroup: Time from onset to randomisation ≥24 h

domains.notes: Central randomisation, stratified by hospital and pre-stroke antihypertensive use; allocation concealed; baseline characteristics well balanced.
Treating clinicians unblinded; outcome assessors and patients blinded; blinded endpoint adjudication reduces detection bias.
3-month follow-up data available for 1988 intervention and 1987 control (50 and 46 missing, respectively). Missing data relatively low. Primary analysis was ITT.
Intervention achieved sustained BP separation; control contamination: 2.3% of control participants did not discontinue home antihypertensives.
Well balanced: entry SBP 166.7±17.3 vs 165.6±16.5 mm Hg; NIHSS median 4.0 (IQR 2.0–7.0) vs 4.0 (3.0–8.0); age 62.0 vs 62.2 years; 64.4% vs 65.3% men.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate-to-strong internal validity: central randomisation, balanced baseline, blinded endpoint, sustained BP separation, but unblinded treatment delivery and minor control contamination could influence co-interventions.

domains.notes: Represents hospital-treated, predominantly mild-to-moderate acute ischaemic stroke with elevated BP (SBP 140–<220) in a Chinese multicentre setting. Excludes thrombolysis, extreme hypertension, major cardiovascular instability, deep coma.

Most applicable to non-reperfused acute ischaemic stroke; less applicable to thrombolysis/thrombectomy pathways. Background care (e.g., anticoagulant/heparin use) may differ from other health systems.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate generalisability: informs early BP lowering vs withholding in non-thrombolysed acute ischaemic stroke with SBP 140–<220; extrapolation to reperfusion-treated, hyperacute, or very severe cohorts should be cautious.

strengths: Large pragmatic multicentre RCT (n=4071) with clinically important endpoints and high follow-up completeness
Clear and sustained BP separation between groups (~8–9 mm Hg in-hospital SBP differences)
Blinded outcome assessment and adjudication for functional endpoints
Explicit comparison of an 'active BP-lowering strategy' versus 'temporary discontinuation' of antihypertensive drugs, addressing a common real-world decision
limitations: Exclusion of thrombolysis limits relevance to modern reperfusion-heavy pathways
Mean onset-to-randomisation time ~15 hours means the trial does not answer hyperacute (prehospital/first hours) BP-lowering questions
Open-label treatment delivery may influence co-interventions despite blinded endpoints
Stroke severity was generally mild-to-moderate (NIHSS median 4), which may reduce ability to detect effects in severe stroke phenotypes

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted, moderate-to-strong internal validity trial that showed no benefit of early BP reduction in non-reperfused mild-to-moderate acute ischaemic stroke, despite sustained BP separation. The neutral result and exclusion of thrombolysis limit generalisability to reperfusion settings, but the findings support de-escalating routine early antihypertensive intensification in similar patients.
strengths: Large sample size, robust BP separation, blinded endpoint adjudication, pragmatic design
weaknesses: Unblinded clinicians, exclusion of thrombolysis, mild stroke severity, limited generalisability to hyperacute windows

sections.authors_conclusion: CATIS demonstrated that, in non-thrombolysed acute ischaemic stroke within 48 hours and SBP 140–<220 mm Hg, immediate protocolised BP reduction achieves robust physiological separation but does not improve death or functional outcome at either early (14 days/discharge) or standard (3 months) timepoints. The trial’s main value is in de-escalating routine early antihypertensive intensification in this population while sharpening questions about timing and context.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Does not change practice for non-reperfused acute ischaemic stroke: routine early BP reduction to <140/90 does not improve outcomes; temporary withholding of home antihypertensives is safe.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Hospital-treated, non-thrombolysed acute ischaemic stroke patients with SBP 140–<220 mm Hg.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That BP lowering is harmful or that severe hypertension should not be treated; the trial excluded severe hypertension and thrombolysis.
implementation_caveats: Not applicable to patients receiving thrombolysis or thrombectomy
Timing matters: potential benefit if treatment started ≥24 hours after onset (hypothesis-generating)
Stroke severity was mild-to-moderate; effects in severe stroke unknown

controversies.notes: Early BP reduction may compromise penumbral perfusion; CATIS evaluated a mean 15-hour window, not hyperacute.
Systematic reviews of BP-lowering trials in early ischaemic stroke also show no clear functional outcome improvement, supporting CATIS neutrality.
Post-CATIS guidelines recommend against routine BP lowering in acute ischaemic stroke except severe hypertension or thrombolysis/thrombectomy settings, consistent with CATIS findings.

unresolved_questions: Does hyperacute BP lowering (first hours) improve outcomes in acute ischaemic stroke?
What is the optimal BP management in severe stroke (NIHSS >15)?
Does BP management differ in patients receiving thrombolysis or thrombectomy?
Is the time-dependent effect (≥24 hours) real and replicable?

numbers_to_remember: SBP difference at 24h: 144.7 vs 152.9 mm Hg (mean difference -8.1)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In non-thrombolysed acute ischaemic stroke with SBP 140–<220 mm Hg, early BP reduction does not improve functional outcomes; temporary withholding of antihypertensives is safe.
